p: Fifty Strategies, One Semester · a book study for content teachers
t: A department, a grade-level team, or a whole faculty of content teachers who have English learners on their rosters. It works best with eight to twelve people, a copy of the book each, and a fixed slot: the first PLC meeting of every other week for a semester, or every week for two months.

p: Fifty Strategies, One Semester · a book study for content teachers
t: 0–5 Opener. One question, everybody answers in a sentence. No reading required to answer it. 5–10 Bring back. Last week's try-it: two people describe what happened, in two minutes each. Evidence beats opinion: a student sentence, a photo of the board, an exit ticket. 10–30 Discuss. Four questions on the six strategies read. The facilitator's job is to keep the talk on what we would do in our rooms , not on whether the book is right. 30–40 Choose. Each teacher names the one strategy they will try before the next session, the class, and the day. Say it out loud; write it in the log. 40–45 Exit.

p: Fifty Strategies, One Semester · a book study for content teachers
t: Read before you come; the discussion assumes the six strategies. Fifteen to twenty pages a session. One try-it per teacher per session, in a class that has at least one English learner. Small is fine; done is the point. Bring evidence, not a verdict. "Here is what the two newcomers wrote" is worth more than "it went well." The EL specialist attends as a colleague, not the expert. The questions are written so that the content teacher's knowledge of the content is what matters.

h: Finishing the program · Terminar el programa
t: To exit EL services in Mississippi, a student must score Level 4 or 5 in all four domains on the same spring test. One domain at Level 3 means one more year, focused on that domain. After exiting, the school monitors grades and test scores for four years . If your child struggles, services can restart. Exiting does not remove any class your child likes; it removes the EL label and the yearly test. Being an EL student never blocks honors, AP, sports, clubs or graduation. p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: How a second language is actually acquired
t: Five findings from second language acquisition research, and what each one asks you to do differently on Monday. Most of what slows an English learner down in a content classroom is not ability, and it is not effort. It is a mismatch between how we teach language and how language is learned. These five findings have held up across decades of research, and every one of them has a move attached. 1

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: Language is acquired through understanding, not repetition
t: Students acquire English when they understand messages slightly beyond their current level — what Krashen called comprehensible input. Drills and word lists produce recall; understood language produces acquisition. Your move: keep the content the same and make the message reachable — visuals, gestures, examples, a slower rate with normal vocabulary. Never lower the concept to lower the language. 2

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: Silence is a stage, not refusal
t: Newcomers often go through a silent period, absorbing far more than they produce. A student who won't speak in week three may be building the system they'll use in week twelve. Your move: let them show understanding without talking — point, sort, match, draw, thumbs up. Invite speech; don't force it in front of thirty peers. 3

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: The affective filter is real: when students are embarrassed or afraid of being wrong, input stops getting through. Cold calls and public error correction raise that filter fastest. Your move: rehearse answers in pairs before anyone speaks publicly, and respond to meaning first. Learn to pronounce their name correctly — it matters more than any strategy on this page. 4

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: Output is where the gaps show up
t: Swain's work on pushed output holds that producing language forces students to notice what they can't yet say. Comprehension alone will not carry a student to Level 4. Your move: every period, require one extended spoken or written response with a frame to support it. A comprehension check is not output. 5

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: What they know in Spanish transfers to English
t: Cummins' work on transfer holds that concepts and literacy skills cross languages — the idea does not have to be relearned, only relabeled. Your move: let students think, discuss, and pre-write in Spanish on the way to English, and point out cognates — analyze / analizar , evidence / evidencia , hypothesis / hipótesis . 1–3 vs. 5–7 Years to fluency Conversational ease arrives first; the academic language of analysis and argument takes far longer. t: The Sheltered Instruction Observation Protocol (Echevarría, Vogt, and Short) organizes sheltered teaching into eight components. Here is one thing each asks of a content classroom. 1

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: Post a content objective and a language objective for every lesson, and say both out loud. Students should be able to tell a visitor what they're learning and how they'll use language to show it. 2

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: Connect explicitly to what students already know — including schooling from another country — and pre-teach the three key terms the lesson depends on. 3

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: Match your rate to proficiency, define academic terms in the moment, and demonstrate every task before assigning it. Model, then release. 4

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: Teach students how to learn: previewing, chunking, note-taking frames, self-questioning. Scaffold with think-alouds and questions that ask for reasoning, not recall. 5

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: Structure frequent talk about content in pairs and triads, with grouping that changes by task. Aim to talk less than your students do, and allow home-language clarification. 6

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: Give students something to handle, build, sort, or produce that uses all four domains. New vocabulary sticks when it's used, not when it's copied. 7

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: Keep both objectives visibly supported all period, hold engagement high, and pace to the students in front of you rather than the plan on paper. 8

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: Close by reviewing key vocabulary and concepts, give feedback on language and content separately, and check comprehension of all students before they leave. Keep the thinking hard and the language reachable. Scaffolding is not lowering the bar — it's building the stairs.

h: Four to seven years, even in strong programs
t: Long-term studies of academic achievement consistently put full academic English proficiency several years out, well past the point where a student sounds fluent. Program quality shortens the timeline; nothing eliminates it. In your room: judge growth against where the student started, not against a native-speaking peer, and expect scaffolding to be necessary long after conversation is easy. Nation Lexical coverage

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: Comprehension needs about 95 to 98 percent known words
t: Below that threshold, unknown vocabulary crowds out meaning and students cannot guess their way through a passage. Words also need many encounters in context before they stick — one exposure on a list is not one of them. In your room: pre-teach the few words that carry the passage, then recycle them deliberately in your talk, your questions, and the exit ticket. Long, Gass Interaction and negotiation

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: Acquisition accelerates when meaning gets negotiated
t: Input matters most when learners have to work at it with someone — clarifying, confirming, rephrasing. That back-and-forth makes language comprehensible and simultaneously pushes production. In your room: build in structured pair tasks where partners must ask each other something to finish the work, rather than round-robin answers to you. Lyster & Ranta Corrective feedback

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: Recasts feel kind, prompts get repair
t: Their classroom analysis found recasts to be the most common form of feedback and among the least likely to be noticed as correction, while prompts — clarification requests, elicitation, repetition of the error point — produced far more student self-repair. In your room: keep recasting for flow, but when accuracy matters, pause and elicit: "Say that again with the past tense." Let the student make the fix. Want the citations? p: Elementary Newcomer Kit (K–5)
t: Same short phrases every day: “Line up.” “Eyes on me.” “Show me.” Gesture every time. Songs and chants carry grammar for free; use the ones the class already sings. p: Elementary Newcomer Kit (K–5)
t: Spanish, Portuguese, Vietnamese: the alphabet transfers; teach the sounds that differ (short vowels, th, sh). Arabic, Chinese: teach letter shapes with sand, body movement, tracing. Math: numbers and operations transfer almost completely; the word problem is the barrier, not the math. Pair every number with the quantity (dots, cubes) for the first month.

p: Elementary Newcomer Kit (K–5)
h: The four lanes, for little ones
t: Newcomer Weeks 1–8 for most Points, matches, sorts, draws, copies. Says single words and memorized chunks. Needs a buddy and pictures for everything. Emerging Often by mid-year Two- and three-word phrases. Follows routine directions without the gesture. Starts to retell with picture support. Progressing Year two for many Simple sentences about what they see and do. Reads decodable text. Needs vocabulary pre-taught for content. Challenge Near grade-level peers Push for complete sentences, past tense, “because.” Give them the job of explaining to the next newcomer.

p: Elementary Newcomer Kit (K–5)
t: A nine-year-old newcomer is old enough to be embarrassed and young enough to catch up fast. They often read and compute at or above grade level in their first language. Protect their dignity and give them content from day one. Day The one thing to get right What the student does What you hand the family 1 A private tour, a buddy who shares a language if possible, and a way to say “I don't understand” without an audience. p: Elementary Newcomer Kit (K–5)

p: The Writing Studio · write for a 4 or a 5
t: Target The features a top-level ELPA21 writing response shows: a claim that answers the prompt in the prompt's words; two reasons, each with an example or a result; organizing transitions with correct punctuation; the other side acknowledged; a conclusion; a formal register when the task is an email; controlled sentences and clean mechanics. The lessons teach those features; they do not reproduce any scoring document.
